transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s the bridges, really. I mean, I used to drive all over without thinking much of it—my wife and I would take these little trips, and she always liked looking out over the water, you know—but now, if I know a bridge crossing is coming and I can’t avoid it, it hits me right away. My heart starts pounding before I’m even on the thing, and my hands get damp on the steering wheel, or on the armrest if someone else is driving. It’s just this awful rush of fear, like my whole body is shouting at me to get away.
Do you get this same rush of fear in other places besides bridges?

Not really in the same way, no. I mean, I can get uneasy here and there—who doesn’t at my age, with traffic and all that—but that awful rush, the heart pounding and my hands getting damp, that’s when I know a bridge is coming and there’s no way around it. Sometimes it starts before I’m even on the bridge, just knowing I have to cross it. My wife used to say I’d grip the wheel like I was trying to bend it, and I suppose I still do.
Have you ever had one of these sudden rushes of fear when no bridge was involved?

No, I don’t think so—not that same sudden rush. It’s really when a bridge crossing becomes unavoidable. Even before I’m on it, my heart starts pounding and my hands get damp, whether I’m holding the steering wheel or just sitting there with my hand on the armrest. Funny, my wife used to like those scenic routes, the ones over the water, and I used to pretend I was enjoying the view too—but now the moment I know there’s no way around the bridge, it just comes over me.
When you're on a bridge, is the scariest part feeling like you couldn't easily get away or get help if something happened?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, exactly. I mean, I suppose once you’re up there you can’t just turn around, can you? But I don’t know if I’m thinking, “No one can help me,” in so many words.

It’s more just… the bridge is there, and I have to get across it. Though now that you say it, I remember one of those big bridges we used to take years ago—my wife loved that view, all the boats down below—and I’d try to look straight ahead and not make a fuss. But what part of it is the scariest, I don’t know. It’s hard for me to separate it out like that.
When you’re on a bridge, is the thing that frightens you most the bridge itself?

Yes… I suppose it is the bridge itself, more than anything. I know, rationally, thousands of cars go over those bridges every day without a thought. My grandson says you can look it all up on the phone now, traffic cameras and all that—though I never did like fussing with those little screens.

But when I see one of those high spans on the map, or coming up ahead through the windshield, it feels like… like the whole thing is just waiting to drop away underneath us. I know that sounds foolish, but that’s what it feels like.
Do you go out of your way to avoid bridges?

Yes, I do. More than I’d like to admit, really. For over two years now I’ve been planning errands and visits around which roads don’t have bridges. It sounds silly when I say it out loud, but I’ll sit there with a map—well, sometimes my grandson helps with the phone, because those maps talk to you now—and I’ll pick the longer way just to avoid one.

We used to go down to San Juan, and to Seattle for theater nights, my wife and I, and I’ve more or less given those up if it means crossing certain bridges. If there’s absolutely no way around it, I need the whole route figured out ahead of time, the timing just right, and someone with me. And even then I’m just sitting there frightened the whole way across.
Do you also avoid other places where it might be hard to leave, like tunnels or crowded public transportation?

I’m not sure, Doctor. I don’t really think about tunnels or buses the same way, at least not that I’ve noticed.

I mean, I haven’t taken much public transportation in years anyway—my wife and I used to take the ferry sometimes, though that’s not what you asked. Crowds can be a nuisance, of course, but I don’t know that I’m avoiding them because I can’t get out. The bridge is the thing that stands out to me. Tunnels… well, I’d have to think on that.
Do tunnels bring on the same kind of fear for you that bridges do?

Tunnels… I don’t know that they do, not in the same way. I mean, I’ve been through the tunnel downtown a time or two, years back, and I remember more about the traffic than the tunnel itself.

My brother-in-law used to complain about tunnels—said they felt like driving through a drainpipe—but I never really had that thought. With bridges it’s different, or at least it feels different to me. The height, the water underneath, all that open space… tunnels don’t come to mind the same way.

So I suppose my answer is no, or not that I’ve noticed.
